principles: Every input batch is a signed change. The runtime computes only what those changes can reach.
The graph engine stays neutral to health, Azure, Kubernetes, and business language.
Stateless steps map. Stateful steps reduce by a declared key and hide that state behind the operator interface.
GKQL is the sole long-term authored graph language.
Use cases, rules, ontology, and policy live in definitions and projections, not in the engine.
Accepted dashboard answers become GitHub issue comments. The browser stores no durable decision.

metrics.label: Live bytes per master node
metrics.detail: At 1,000,006 master nodes, below the 8 KB limit after compaction.

metrics.label: Writer CPU per record
metrics.detail: At the million-node serial baseline. The project gate is 37 us.

metrics.label: Steady window close
metrics.detail: Median at one million nodes; 4.53 s observed maximum versus a 5 s p99 gate.

metrics.label: Measured Canvas graph
metrics.detail: Nodes in the documented Canvas benchmark, with 287,703 edges.

metrics.label: Canvas at 10^6
metrics.detail: The one-million figure currently belongs to the engine, not the browser renderer.

findings.title: The runtime still owns domain policy through the authoring adapter
findings.summary: The engine graph operators are neutral, but the adapter registry and AuthoringAdapter still compile health, curation, capability, and Azure-specific contracts into the runtime.
findings.principle: Use cases and policy live in projections; the engine only understands typed rows and generic operators.

evidence.detail: AdapterRegistry hard-codes built-in adapters, including AuthoringAdapter.
AuthoringAdapter declares a domain-specific SignalRuleRow contract.
The runtime recognizes sattle.authoring when reasoning about telemetry source coverage.

findings.question: Should the existing authoring wire format move unchanged behind an optional adapter module, or be replaced by generic record rows plus an alias?

options.title: Move the adapter unchanged
options.detail: Preserve captures, journals, IDs, diagnostics, and compatibility while removing the contracts from core Runtime.

options.title: Replace with generic record inputs
options.detail: Declare validation in modules and keep sattle.authoring only as a migration alias.

findings.recommendation: Move the existing adapter unchanged first. Generic records are a separate follow-up after compatibility is proven.
verification: A space without sattle.authoring constructs no adapter that exposes a health row type.
Existing captures and journals replay with equal graph data and diagnostics.
A planted SignalRuleRow token in guarded assemblies fails the architecture test.

findings.title: The product still has two definition frontends and two projection languages
findings.summary: GKQL reads modules and projections, while .sattle, KQL, printers, protocol text, and historical journals remain active paths. The migration plan is right, but the completion boundary is spread across many issues.
findings.principle: GKQL is the one long-term authored graph language; compatibility tooling is a migration implementation, not the product model.

evidence.detail: IProjectionSource is the shared seam below different projection languages.
The catalog's directory reader loads definition text; the preceding contract still names .sattle modules.
GKQL already has a module reader. The remaining authoring migration is owned by #132, with corpus and store parity in #129 and #131.

findings.question: Should S2 removal happen as one release gate, or should the legacy reader become a pinned external migration artifact as soon as corpus parity lands?

options.title: S0 warning, S1 writer cutover, S2 removal
options.detail: Preserve a short compatibility window and remove the reader only after #129 and #131.

options.title: Move the reader out immediately after parity
options.detail: Keep the legacy parser only in a pinned migration binary, with no normal product path.

findings.recommendation: Use the three stages, but make the pinned migration artifact the only S2 owner.
verification: GKQL read-print-read is stable and byte-stable.
No product code path reads .sattle at S2.
Historical stores and releases upgrade through the pinned artifact.

findings.title: The documented change algebra is not the algebra the runtime executes
findings.summary: Core/Algebra describes Delta and Squash, while execution uses columnar weighted batches, Graph patches, and WindowChange records. That is valid only if the paper calls it specification rather than implementation.
findings.principle: One named executable change contract should connect source rows, operator state, graph patches, telemetry, and tests.

evidence.detail: Core.Patch implements the chapter 4 mathematical patch representation.
Runtime batches expose signed row weights, defaulting to +1 when no weight column is needed.
RunEpoch transports GraphDelta, a patch plus state plus telemetry, not Core.Delta.

findings.question: Should Core.Delta become the actual interchange contract, or should it be renamed and documented as the proof specification?

options.title: Make the algebra executable
options.detail: Converge the runtime on one change representation and prove operator equivalence.

options.title: Make the algebra explicitly spec-only
options.detail: Rename GraphDelta and document the distinct runtime plan so readers cannot infer execution from the theory layer.

findings.recommendation: Do not pay the convergence cost before the scale gates settle. Mark the current algebra spec-only and rename the runtime concept.
verification: The paper and README name the runtime and proof representations explicitly.
No module exposes both Delta meanings through one public contract.
Differential tests state which representation they prove.

findings.title: Partitionable-by-key is a design goal, not an implemented engine property
findings.summary: The engine remains a single-writer topological loop. Parallel work exists only inside Match preparation. The project cannot yet claim key-partitioned incremental execution.
findings.principle: The core computes on reached keys and windows; a future partition boundary must preserve ordered epochs and atomic publication.

evidence.detail: RunEpoch owns ordered evaluation of graphs. This is not a distributed key-partitioned executor.
The host exposes one synchronization gate around its lifecycle.
Untouched graphs are skipped when no upstream patch, telemetry or time-dependent work reaches them.

findings.question: Is the intended partition unit a state key inside one engine, or a whole graph space owned by a grain/process?

options.title: Partition graph spaces first
options.detail: Keep one ordered writer per space and scale independent spaces before splitting one projection network.

options.title: Partition state by declared key
options.detail: Split stateful operators now and preserve a merged commit frontier per graph.

findings.recommendation: Partition independent spaces first. It matches the current ownership model and avoids exposing key ownership through every operator.
verification: Public docs distinguish current single-writer behavior from future partitioning.
One benchmark names per-space and per-key throughput separately.
Ordered publication and idempotent recovery are proved before key splitting.

findings.title: Definition reactivation replays history through a fresh engine
findings.summary: Drafts and committed definition changes build a new engine and replay retained inputs. This is correct and simple, but it makes authoring cost proportional to history and ties preview to retention and the shared interner.
findings.principle: A deep module may hide expensive recomputation, but the interface must state retention, time, and preview consequences.

evidence.anchor: (Engine Engine, long Rows, bool Complete) Reactivate(
evidence.detail: Reactivate constructs a fresh engine and replays inputs, subject to a row limit.
Reactivation reads retained inputs, falling back to the journal.
Engine construction receives the host's shared interner. Candidate/live isolation needs an explicit contract.

findings.question: Should preview remain full replay with a documented budget, or should changed projections update incrementally from a retained checkpoint?

options.title: Keep full replay with a strict budget
options.detail: Simplest correctness path; expose row limits, elapsed time, and interruption state.

options.title: Introduce checkpointed activation deltas
options.detail: More complex, but makes authoring cost follow changed definition reach instead of all history.

findings.recommendation: Keep full replay through the GKQL cutover. Revisit incrementality only after the preview budget is measured.
verification: Preview and commit share a public reactivation budget contract.
Shared interner behavior is tested under different batch cuts.
A journalless row-cap failure is actionable and non-destructive.

findings.title: Telemetry implementations leak through the nominal store interface
findings.summary: The runtime exposes a telemetry port, but several callers cast to the in-memory implementation and state digests only include what that concrete store can enumerate.
findings.principle: One deep store interface should own retention, enumeration, comparison, and recovery invariants.

evidence.detail: ITelemetryStore declares the persistence seam.
Digest code reaches concrete in-memory telemetry state.

evidence.anchor: if (engine.Telemetry is not InMemoryTelemetryStore mem) yield break;
evidence.detail: This export path yields no telemetry for a non-memory implementation.

findings.question: Should the port grow an enumeration/proof interface, or should digest/export read a new derived telemetry snapshot module?

options.title: Deepen the telemetry store interface
options.detail: The store owns scans, retained windows, digests, and recovery snapshots.

options.title: Add a derived telemetry snapshot
options.detail: Keep persistence narrow and build one portable view for digest, export, and preview.

findings.recommendation: Deepen the existing store interface. A second snapshot module would duplicate retention and time invariants.
verification: In-memory and SQLite implementations pass the same digest/export contract tests.
No production cast depends on InMemoryTelemetryStore.
Retention behavior is explicit for derived graph state.

findings.title: Incremental means reached changes, but operator cost still needs an explicit budget
findings.summary: RunEpoch skips untouched graphs, yet a reached graph may traverse and retain state proportional to its keys, series, or neighbourhood. The project needs a cost contract per operator, not only end-to-end timings.
findings.principle: Each operator should know exactly which keys, windows, and elements an input change can touch.

evidence.detail: Graphs step only when upstream changes or time-dependent work reaches them.

evidence.anchor: public readonly Table Rows; public readonly Arrangement ByKey;
evidence.detail: Join retains rows and a keyed arrangement. This bounds lookup shape, but is not a measured cost guarantee.

evidence.anchor: Match over a graph port, incremental by the bilinear delta rule
evidence.detail: Match documents its incremental bilinear delta rule for changed components.

findings.question: Which operator cost promises should become release gates: touched keys, changed windows, graph degree, or total retained series?

options.title: Gate by reached keys and windows
options.detail: Preserves the intended incremental contract and catches full scans even when end-to-end input is small.

options.title: Keep only end-to-end scale gates
options.detail: Simpler now, but allows regressions to hide behind a particular fixture and machine.

findings.recommendation: Add touched-key/window counters per operator while retaining end-to-end gates.
verification: Every stateful operator reports the keys, windows, and elements examined.
A sparse one-change case fails if an unrelated region is scanned.
The 1M end-to-end gates remain unchanged.

findings.title: Engine scale evidence does not establish Canvas capacity
findings.summary: The repository proves about one million engine master nodes, while Canvas evidence stops near 100,000 nodes. The renderer may be capable of more, but capacity is currently unmeasured.
findings.principle: A claim names one module, one workload, one hardware profile, and the measured percentile or failure mode.

evidence.detail: The documented Canvas target is 100,000 nodes and 300,000 edges.
The measured fixture has 99,495 nodes and 287,703 edges.

evidence.anchor: | Memory held, after a full garbage collection |
evidence.detail: The engine scale table reports memory per master node. It is not a browser renderer measurement.

findings.question: After the first five one-million Canvas runs, should the product gate be 30 fps or 60 fps p50?

options.title: Gate the initial 1M tier at 30 fps
options.detail: Sets an evidence-consistent first tier while panning a much larger scene.

options.title: Gate the 1M tier at 60 fps
options.detail: Matches the 100k target and makes the capacity claim easier to explain.

findings.recommendation: Start at 30 fps, then publish a separate 60 fps stretch if the data supports it.
verification: A client-only 1M preset runs five times on pinned hardware.
Load, layout, GPU upload, heap, pan, zoom, pick, patch, OOM, and context loss are recorded.
No Canvas 1M claim appears before the table exists.

findings.title: Canvas graph views share a scene design but not a context lifecycle
findings.summary: Large graph views already converge on GraphView, but each pane creates a WebGL context and context loss is unhandled. This is a lifecycle and budget problem before it is a Three.js problem.
findings.principle: Use one narrow scene interface. Change the backend only when a measured renderer-attributed failure justifies it.

evidence.detail: GraphRenderer owns WebGL2 programs, buffers and texture state.
Each GraphRenderer acquires its own WebGL2 context.
GraphView combines WebGL geometry with a bounded Canvas2D label overlay.

findings.question: Should multiple panes use capped per-pane contexts with eviction, or one shared multi-viewport canvas?

options.title: Cap contexts and evict inactive panes
options.detail: Preserves current GraphView structure and uses the context-restoration path.

options.title: Use one multi-viewport canvas
options.detail: Reduces contexts but changes picking, camera, labels, and focus ownership across panes.

findings.recommendation: Cap at 12 contexts and evict inactive panes. Do not replace the renderer with Three.js without a failing measured profile.
verification: Twenty panes never exceed 12 active contexts.
webglcontextlost/restored restores camera, selection, buffers, and textures.
No full-graph DOM representation is introduced.

findings.title: Operational /health and model health currently share a word but not a concept
findings.summary: The /health endpoint reports process, sequence, digest, graph, and source lag. Domain health is computed by projections. The concepts are different, and the name encourages accidental coupling.
findings.principle: Names at a public interface should describe invariants and owners, not the nearest use case.

evidence.detail: The HTTP /health endpoint is operational liveness and journal status, not domain model health.
Legacy count syntax does embed domain-state labels into language metadata. This is separate from the operational endpoint name.

findings.question: Should the endpoint remain /health for compatibility, be renamed to /status, or expose /status with /health as an alias?

options.title: Add /status and retain /health
options.detail: Clarifies new callers without breaking monitoring integrations.

options.title: Keep /health operationally
options.detail: Avoid churn and enforce a contract test that model state never enters the payload.

findings.recommendation: Keep /health stable and pin its key set. Use clearer terminology in code and docs rather than a URL rename.
verification: The response key set contains only operational fields.
No domain state label is imported or emitted by the endpoint.
The protocol documents the distinction.

findings.title: SpaceHost is becoming the owner of every lifecycle under one lock
findings.summary: Host combines journal, replay, live envelopes, engine activation, served history, protocol publication, drafts, and persistence coordination. Its change count is a hotspot signal, not proof that its deep lifecycle boundary should be split.
findings.principle: A deep module hides complexity, but it should expose one narrow lifecycle interface instead of making callers know all of its internal phases.

evidence.detail: A single gate coordinates the host lifecycle.
Accept owns journal-first then apply sequencing for inputs.

evidence.anchor: var cand = Candidate(changed, out var res, out _);
evidence.detail: Draft preview reaches candidate activation. Any split must preserve the same ordering and recovery invariants.

findings.question: Should Host remain one deep lifecycle module with internal collaborators, or be split into activation, publication, and persistence modules?

options.title: Keep Host, add private collaborators
options.detail: Preserve the lifecycle seam and test it publicly while concentrating invariants internally.

options.title: Expose separate modules
options.detail: Creates additional caller-visible ordering and recovery contracts, with more concurrency risk.

findings.recommendation: Deepen Host internally. Do not expose protocol, journal, or activation modules until at least two adapters require that public seam.
verification: Crash, retry, and reactivation tests remain at the SpaceHost interface.
No new public phase enum or pass-through module appears.
Journal, publication, and preview invariants stay covered by one lifecycle test.
